issues.description: The manuscript contains a fundamental and critical contradiction in the sample description. The Methods section states participants were recruited through 'the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington' with an average age of 19 years and 68% female, which is clearly a student convenience sample. However, the Abstract, Discussion, and Conclusion repeatedly describe this as a 'national probability sample' or 'nationally representative sample.' These are mutually exclusive descriptions. A university psychology participant pool is neither nationally representative nor a probability sample. This contradiction undermines the entire framing of the study and its claimed advantages over prior student-sample research.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington... the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The paper repeatedly claims the sample is a 'national probability sample' and 'nationally representative,' and uses this as a key argument for why results differ from prior student-sample studies. However, the sample is drawn from an introductory psychology pool at a single university, is predominantly young (M=19), predominantly female (68%), predominantly Pākehā (86%), and is therefore highly unrepresentative of the New Zealand general population. The entire theoretical argument that SDO (rather than RWA) is the stronger predictor in general population samples is built on this false premise. The Discussion section states 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population,' which is directly contradicted by the sample characteristics.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The Abstract and Current Study section state the study examines 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment,' yet the Measures section describes environmentalism as 'participants' concern about environmental problems' using items about concern and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. These are distinct constructs: behavioral intention/willingness is not the same as attitudinal concern. The Results and Discussion sections then refer to 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment' (WILL). Three different operationalizations are used across sections for what is presented as a single outcome variable, creating serious construct validity ambiguity.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'.

issues.description: The environmentalism measure is described as having items modelled from Liu and Sibley's scale, but only two items are mentioned. It is unclear how many items total comprise the scale, what the full item set is, how the reverse-scored item ('problems have been exaggerated') was handled, and what the reliability of this measure is. No Cronbach's alpha or omega is reported for the environmentalism scale in Table 1 (the diagonal appears to show .76 but this is not confirmed in text). This prevents evaluation of measurement quality and replication.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'.

issues.description: The paper states 374 participants were included across five time points but provides no information about the total number recruited, dropout rates at each wave, or whether the 374 represents completers only. The paper states 'Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website,' which is inadequate for peer review. Attrition patterns are critical for evaluating whether listwise deletion (the stated analysis approach) introduces systematic bias, particularly given the five-year span.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European). Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The authors state analyses were conducted using listwise deletion across five time points over five years. With five waves of data, listwise deletion is likely to produce substantial reduction in sample size and, more critically, non-random attrition bias (those who drop out over five years likely differ systematically from completers on the key variables of interest). Full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation would be more appropriate and are standard practice for longitudinal panel data. The authors do not report how many participants had complete data across all five waves versus the original recruited sample.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: The RMSEA 90% confidence interval is reported as [.025, .026], which is an implausibly narrow interval (a range of only .001) for a model of this complexity. This appears to be a reporting error, likely a copy-paste mistake or typographical error. A realistic RMSEA CI would span a wider range. This calls into question the accuracy of other reported statistics.

The results report regression coefficients with 'SD' values (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'), but in the context of regression coefficients, this should be labeled 'SE' (standard error), not 'SD' (standard deviation). Standard deviation and standard error are distinct statistics. This is either a systematic labeling error throughout the results or reflects a conceptual confusion between the two statistics.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The reported confidence interval for the RWA-to-environmentalism path is [-.05, -.01], but the point estimate is B = -.02. This CI is asymmetric around the point estimate (-.02 is not centered between -.05 and -.01; the distance from -.05 to -.02 is .03, while from -.02 to -.01 is .01). While asymmetric CIs can occur with bootstrapping, this asymmetry is unusually large relative to the point estimate and warrants explanation. Similarly, the CI for the lagged effect of environmentalism on RWA is [-.01, -.003] with B = -.01, which means the upper bound equals the point estimate, which is impossible for a standard CI.

The chi-square difference test comparing the SDO-to-RWA cross-lagged path constraint yields χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001. This is an extraordinarily large chi-square value for a single degree of freedom test in a model with 374 participants. Such a value would be implausible under normal circumstances and suggests either a computational error, a misreported statistic, or a fundamental problem with the model specification. For context, the overall model chi-square is χ²(2279) = 36,511.73, meaning this single df test accounts for nearly half the total model chi-square, which is statistically impossible in a properly specified nested model comparison.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001), a finding we explore more fully in the Discussion.

issues.description: The RWA scale had a different number of items at Time 2 compared to all other time points ('The item... was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points'). This creates measurement non-invariance across waves, which is a serious problem for a cross-lagged model that constrains parameters to be time-invariant (stationary). The authors do not test for or acknowledge measurement invariance, and do not explain how this missing item was handled analytically. Comparing latent or composite scores across time points when the measure differs is methodologically problematic.
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The cross-lagged panel model assumes that constructs are measured equivalently across all five time points (measurement invariance). The authors do not report any tests of configural, metric, or scalar invariance. Without establishing measurement invariance, it is impossible to determine whether observed changes over time reflect true changes in the constructs or changes in how participants interpret and respond to items. This is a fundamental requirement for longitudinal structural equation modeling.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The authors use a traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) without acknowledging its well-documented limitations. The CLPM does not control for stable trait-like between-person differences, meaning the cross-lagged paths may reflect between-person differences rather than within-person change. The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015) is now considered the appropriate alternative. The authors' causal claims about SDO influencing environmentalism over time are particularly vulnerable to this critique, as stable individual differences in both variables could produce spurious cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: Despite using a cross-lagged panel design (which cannot establish causation), the authors make strong causal claims throughout the Discussion. The paper states 'These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism' and 'this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.' Cross-lagged associations in observational panel data do not establish causation, particularly without controlling for unmeasured confounders or using experimental manipulation.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism... With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.description: The Methods section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' but Figure 1 states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are inconsistent thresholds. The use of p < .01 as the threshold in Figure 1 is more stringent than the stated p < .05, and the rationale for using p < .01 (rather than the stated p < .05) is not explained.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings... All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: Figure 1 is referenced throughout the Results section as the primary source for autoregressive and cross-lagged path coefficients, but the figure itself is not included in the manuscript text provided. All autoregressive paths are described as shown in Figure 1 without being reported numerically in the text. This means the stability coefficients, which are central to the paper's first hypothesis, cannot be evaluated by reviewers.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

issues.description: The authors report poor CFI (.86, below the conventional .90 or .95 threshold) and dismiss it by noting it is 'affected by model complexity,' then accept the model based on RMSEA and SRMR alone. No justification is provided for why complexity-affected indices should be disregarded, and no sensitivity analyses or alternative model specifications are reported. The decision to accept a model with CFI = .86 requires more rigorous justification, particularly given the stationary constraints imposed.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The study involves multiple analytical decisions (choice of stationary vs. non-stationary model, listwise deletion, significance thresholds, which cross-lagged paths to constrain) with no mention of pre-registration. The post-hoc model comparison testing whether SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA, and the interpretation of non-significant chi-square difference tests as supporting the authors' preferred interpretation, raise concerns about analytic flexibility. The paper does not disclose whether these analytical choices were made a priori or after examining the data.
issues.quote: Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible. Instead, we imposed similar constraints on the model as in the Wald test... We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor.

issues.description: The authors conduct a chi-square difference test to compare whether SDO and RWA paths to environmentalism are equal, find a non-significant result (χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126), and then interpret this as supporting their claim that SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA. A non-significant chi-square difference test means the data are consistent with the paths being equal—it does not provide evidence that they differ. The authors acknowledge this but then proceed to interpret the pattern of coefficients as meaningful, which is circular reasoning given the formal test failed to reject equality.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: Both SDO and RWA are measured with only six items each from their respective full scales. The authors acknowledge 'Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used.' However, they do not report what the actual reliability values are for SDO and RWA (only the diagonal value for WILL = .76 is visible in Table 1), nor do they discuss the implications of reduced reliability for attenuation of cross-lagged paths. Reduced reliability systematically attenuates observed associations, which is particularly problematic when comparing the relative strength of SDO vs. RWA paths if the two scales have different reliabilities.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: The paper does not explicitly report Cronbach's alpha or other reliability estimates for SDO and RWA at any time point, despite acknowledging that reliabilities are 'poorer than is typically the case.' Table 1 appears to show diagonal values that may represent reliabilities, but this is not labeled or explained in the table note. Reliability information is essential for evaluating measurement quality and interpreting the magnitude of observed associations.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: The paper references the NZAVS (New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study) website for sample details and states the Mplus syntax will be available there. However, the Methods section describes recruitment through 'the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington,' which is not the NZAVS (a national longitudinal study of adult New Zealanders). This suggests either the sample is misidentified, or the paper conflates two different datasets. The NZAVS is a genuine national probability sample of adult New Zealanders, while the described sample is a student pool—these cannot be the same dataset.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website... A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: The Introduction states that Stanley et al. [14] found 'RWA, and not SDO, predicts an increase in climate change denial' in a student sample. The current paper then argues its general population sample should show SDO as the stronger predictor based on Stanley and Wilson's [22] meta-analysis. However, the current sample is also a student sample (introductory psychology pool, mean age 19), making the predicted pattern inconsistent with the authors' own theoretical framework, which predicts SDO should be stronger only in general population samples.
issues.quote: Stanley et al. [14] examined the association between endorsement of RWA, SDO and environmentalism over time using a student sample surveyed twice over five months. They found that RWA, and not SDO, predicts an increase in climate change denial... The present paper advances this research by examining the impact of SDO and RWA on environment-related attitudes in a general population sample, spanning five years.

issues.description: The study spans five years across five time points described as 'five semesters,' but the paper does not specify the exact timing of each wave or whether the intervals between waves are equal. Cross-lagged panel models with stationary (time-invariant) constraints assume equal time intervals between waves. If the intervals between semesters vary (e.g., due to academic calendar differences), the stationarity assumption is violated and the constrained model is misspecified.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: Descriptive statistics (means, SDs, correlations) are only reported for Time 1. For a five-wave longitudinal study, descriptive statistics at each wave are necessary to evaluate whether the variables change over time, to assess potential floor/ceiling effects, and to evaluate the plausibility of the stationary model assumption. The absence of this information prevents adequate evaluation of the data.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.description: The Discussion states the current pattern 'is the reverse of the pattern obtained from the first longitudinal analysis on this topic, which showed that RWA was the stronger predictor among students.' However, the Introduction states that Stanley et al. [14] found 'RWA, and not SDO, predicts an increase in climate change denial, while neither variable is related to changes in pro-environmental attitudes over time.' The outcome variable in Stanley et al. was climate change denial, not willingness to sacrifice for the environment. Comparing these as equivalent outcomes conflates distinct constructs.
issues.quote: This pattern of results, where SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA, is the reverse of the pattern obtained from the first longitudinal analysis on this topic, which showed that RWA was the stronger predictor among students [14].

issues.description: The authors acknowledge in the Discussion that 'a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable' such as economic factors. However, no confounders are controlled for in the analysis. Political orientation, socioeconomic status, media consumption, and major environmental events during 2009-2013 (e.g., the Christchurch earthquake, global financial crisis) are all plausible confounders that could drive both ideological and environmental attitude change. The acknowledgment of this limitation is insufficient given the causal language used throughout.
issues.quote: Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable.

issues.description: The authors describe using 'path analysis' but the model involves multiple items per construct with constraints on residual variances, which suggests a structural equation model with latent variables or a composite-based path model. It is unclear whether latent variables were used or observed composites. This distinction matters for interpreting the results, as latent variable models correct for measurement error while composite-based models do not. The description of constraining 'residual variance for the same item over time' suggests item-level modeling, but this is not clearly explained.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment... We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: The Discussion states 'both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA.' However, the Results section explicitly states that the chi-square difference test comparing these paths was non-significant (χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126), meaning the formal test did not support the claim that SDO is 'significantly' stronger. The Discussion overstates the statistical evidence.
issues.quote: In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA.

issues.description: The model has χ²(2279) = 36,511.73. With only three variables across five time points in a path model, the degrees of freedom of 2279 are extremely large and suggest either a very complex model specification (possibly item-level modeling with many parameters) or an error in reporting. The authors do not provide sufficient model specification details to evaluate whether this df value is correct, and the extremely poor chi-square fit (ratio of approximately 16:1) is not adequately addressed.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86)
